When k-means works—and what it can miss

15 reproducible examples, including all five distinct cases in your supplied slides. Every row shows the same observations: generating groups → unlabelled input → k-means assignments.

All stages remain visible for review; download or copy individual figures to build your slide reveals. Each PNG is 1290 × 1050 pixels (300 DPI). Scroll rows horizontally on smaller screens.

Ground truth is used only for the left panel, evaluation, and matching display colors after fitting. It is never supplied to k-means. Cluster names are arbitrary. Black × marks are fitted centers. Within each row, coordinates and equal axis scales match exactly. These are synthetic illustrations, not digitizations of slide points.

ARI and Rand index compare pairs of observations. The first five rows reproduce the slide examples qualitatively. Added cases are labeled below. Standard fits use k-means++ with 50 starts; the initialization demonstration deliberately uses one poor start.

1. Separated round groups

PDF pages 1–3 · slide 11

A favorable case: similarly sized, compact groups are well separated. A nearby mean is a useful summary of each group.

n = 160 · k = 2 · ARI = 1.000 · Rand index = 1.000 · Data CSV

Fit details

Sum of squared distances = 56.047; 50 initialization(s); 2 iterations for the selected fit. Compare this objective only for the same observations and feature scaling.

2. Unequal spread

PDF pages 4–5 · slide 12

Both groups contain 90 observations, but one is much more diffuse. The nearest-center boundary gives some diffuse-group points to the compact group. Equal spread is helpful, not a formal requirement.

n = 180 · k = 2 · ARI = 0.934 · Rand index = 0.967 · Data CSV

Fit details

Sum of squared distances = 266.457; 50 initialization(s); 5 iterations for the selected fit. Compare this objective only for the same observations and feature scaling.

3. Unequal group sizes

PDF pages 6–7 · slide 13

The generating groups have the same population spread but 10 versus 300 observations. K-means can reduce total squared error by splitting the large group and grouping the small population with part of it.

n = 310 · k = 2 · ARI = 0.016 · Rand index = 0.509 · Data CSV

Fit details

Sum of squared distances = 659.809; 50 initialization(s); 27 iterations for the selected fit. Compare this objective only for the same observations and feature scaling.

4. Long, narrow groups

PDF pages 8–9 · slide 14

The generating groups are the left and right columns. Their large vertical spread makes a top-versus-bottom partition cheaper in squared distance. K-means does not identify groups from their shape alone.

n = 180 · k = 2 · ARI = 0.009 · Rand index = 0.505 · Data CSV

Fit details

Sum of squared distances = 881.247; 50 initialization(s); 7 iterations for the selected fit. Compare this objective only for the same observations and feature scaling.

5. Overlapping groups

PDF pages 10–12 · slide 15

The generating populations overlap. The algorithm creates a hard nearest-center boundary, but nearby observations can have different hidden origins. Even a sensible geometric split cannot perfectly recover those labels.

n = 180 · k = 2 · ARI = 0.412 · Rand index = 0.706 · Data CSV

Fit details

Sum of squared distances = 162.764; 50 initialization(s); 10 iterations for the selected fit. Compare this objective only for the same observations and feature scaling.

6. Two interlocking moons

Additional teaching example

Two curved groups are easy to follow by eye. With two centers, k-means uses a straight dividing boundary and cuts across the moons.

n = 180 · k = 2 · ARI = 0.257 · Rand index = 0.629 · Data CSV

Fit details

Sum of squared distances = 73.081; 50 initialization(s); 7 iterations for the selected fit. Compare this objective only for the same observations and feature scaling.

7. Nested rings

Additional teaching example

The hidden groups are the inner and outer rings. K-means divides space into nearest-center regions, so it cuts across both rings instead of separating inside from outside.

n = 180 · k = 2 · ARI = -0.005 · Rand index = 0.497 · Data CSV

Fit details

Sum of squared distances = 69.258; 50 initialization(s); 7 iterations for the selected fit. Compare this objective only for the same observations and feature scaling.

8. Choosing k: too few

Additional teaching example

These data were generated from three compact groups. Asking for two clusters forces k-means to merge two of them.

n = 180 · k = 2 · ARI = 0.569 · Rand index = 0.777 · Data CSV

Fit details

Sum of squared distances = 933.917; 50 initialization(s); 2 iterations for the selected fit. Compare this objective only for the same observations and feature scaling.

9. Choosing k: a good match

Additional teaching example

The same points with k=3: one center per generating group. This is the reference for the k=2, k=4, and poor-initialization examples.

n = 180 · k = 3 · ARI = 1.000 · Rand index = 1.000 · Data CSV

Fit details

Sum of squared distances = 49.401; 50 initialization(s); 2 iterations for the selected fit. Compare this objective only for the same observations and feature scaling.

10. Choosing k: too many

Additional teaching example

The same points with k=4: one generating group is split. Extra centers reduce squared error, so a lower objective alone does not establish the right number of groups.

n = 180 · k = 4 · ARI = 0.883 · Rand index = 0.950 · Data CSV

Fit details

Sum of squared distances = 42.614; 50 initialization(s); 5 iterations for the selected fit. Compare this objective only for the same observations and feature scaling.

11. A poor initialization

Additional teaching example

The same three-group dataset, but a deliberately poor starting arrangement and only one run. Two centers stay in one group while one center serves the other two. Compare the objective with the multi-start k=3 result above; multiple starts help, but do not guarantee a global optimum.

n = 180 · k = 3 · ARI = 0.440 · Rand index = 0.721 · Data CSV

Fit details

Sum of squared distances = 957.106; 1 initialization(s); 8 iterations for the selected fit. Compare this objective only for the same observations and feature scaling.

12. Feature scaling: original units

Additional teaching example

The groups differ in feature 1, but feature 2 has a much larger numerical range. Raw Euclidean distances are dominated by feature 2, so k-means splits along that variation.

n = 140 · k = 2 · ARI = -0.007 · Rand index = 0.496 · Data CSV

Fit details

Sum of squared distances = 688.980; 50 initialization(s); 3 iterations for the selected fit. Compare this objective only for the same observations and feature scaling.

13. Feature scaling: standardized

Additional teaching example

The same observations after standardizing each feature to unit variance. All three panels show standardized coordinates, exactly as supplied to k-means. Scaling recovers the generating groups here; it changes the question and is not universally the right choice.

n = 140 · k = 2 · ARI = 1.000 · Rand index = 1.000 · Data CSV

Fit details

Sum of squared distances = 141.056; 50 initialization(s); 2 iterations for the selected fit. Compare this objective only for the same observations and feature scaling.

14. One distant outlier

Additional teaching example

The grey point is a designated outlier, not a third generating group. K-means has no reject option: it uses one of the two centers for that point and merges the two main groups. The reported agreement scores exclude the outlier; the fit includes it.

n = 121 · k = 2 · ARI = 0.000 · Rand index = 0.496 · scores on inliers only · Data CSV

Fit details

Sum of squared distances = 524.867; 50 initialization(s); 2 iterations for the selected fit. Compare this objective only for the same observations and feature scaling.

15. Clusters without separate populations

Additional teaching example

All observations come from one Gaussian population. K-means still returns three groups when asked. Colored partitions alone are not evidence for distinct underlying populations.

n = 160 · k = 3 · ARI = 0.000 · Rand index = 0.336 · Data CSV

Fit details

Sum of squared distances = 152.664; 50 initialization(s); 14 iterations for the selected fit. Compare this objective only for the same observations and feature scaling.
